Editorial rewrite of advisor and client prose; substance unchanged.

advisor.summary: Section 1202 excludes gain on qualified small business stock — original-issuance C corporation shares in an active qualified business — and OBBBA split the regime in two. Stock acquired after July 4, 2025 earns a tiered exclusion (50% at a three-year hold, 75% at four, 100% at five or more) under a $15 million or 10-times-basis per-issuer cap and a $75 million gross-asset ceiling; stock acquired before July 5, 2025 keeps the old rules — a strict five-year cliff, a $10 million/10x cap, and a $50 million ceiling, with 100% exclusion for post-September 27, 2010 acquisitions. The partial tiers are not free: a 7% AMT preference and 28%-rate tax on the included portion mean the headline percentage overstates each tier's value. The controlling reality is evidentiary — qualification is fixed at issuance yet tested years later at exam, so the proof file is built at the front end, not the exit. The model removes the eligible amount from recognized long-term gain up to the $15 million cap; it does not compute the tiers, the AMT preference, or the 28%-rate remainder.
mechanics: Qualification locks in at issuance: a domestic C corporation whose aggregate gross assets stay at or below the ceiling ($75M for post-OBBBA issuances; $50M for pre-July 5, 2025 stock) at and immediately after issuance, with shares acquired at original issuance for money, property, or services (§1202(c), (d)) — secondary-market purchases never qualify.

The active-business test of §1202(e) demands at least 80% of assets used in a qualified trade for substantially all of the holding period, with the excluded service fields — health, law, accounting, consulting, financial services, hospitality, farming — litigated at the margins.

Holding-period tiers: post-July 4, 2025 stock earns a 50% exclusion at three years, 75% at four, and 100% at five or more; pre-July 5, 2025 stock faces a five-year cliff with no partial credit — 100% if acquired after September 27, 2010, 75% or 50% for older vintages.

The per-issuer cap under §1202(b) is the greater of the dollar cap ($15M for post-OBBBA stock, indexed after 2026; $10M for older stock) or ten times the aggregate adjusted basis of stock sold that year — the 10x arm rewards high-basis property contributions at incorporation.

Partial tiers carry real costs: 7% of the excluded gain is an AMT preference under §57(a)(7), and the included portion is taxed as 28%-rate gain rather than ordinary LTCG — the effective saving runs well below the headline percentage.

§1202(h) treats gift and death transferees as original holders with tacked holding periods — the foundation for multiplying per-taxpayer caps through genuine, well-in-advance gifts to family members or non-grantor trusts; §1045 permits a 60-day rollover into replacement QSBS when a sale arrives before the tier is reached.

The model applies the exclusion by removing the eligible amount from recognized long-term gain, clamped at the $15M cap — the entered figure must already be the post-tier excludable amount, because tiers, the AMT preference, and the 28%-rate remainder sit outside the transform.

authority.note: The two-regime exclusion: 50/75/100% tiers at 3/4/5-year holds, a $15M (indexed)/10x cap, and a $75M asset ceiling for post-July 4, 2025 issuances; prior law preserved for older stock.
The per-issuer limitation — the greater of the dollar cap or 10x the basis of stock disposed of during the year.
The original-issuance requirement, the gross-asset ceiling at issuance, and the 80% active qualified business test with its excluded service fields.
Gift and death transfers preserve qualification and tack the holding period — the statutory footing for cap multiplication.
Makes 7% of excluded gain an AMT preference on the partial (50%/75%) tiers.
Permits a 60-day rollover into replacement QSBS when a sale lands before the exclusion tier is reached.

requirements: Original-issuance C corporation stock backed by contemporaneous documentation — issuance records, a gross-assets balance sheet at the issuance date, and the capitalization history.
The corporation meets the active-business and non-excluded-field tests for substantially all of the holding period, with no disqualifying redemptions around issuance.
The holding period satisfied lot by lot at sale — three, four, or five years for post-OBBBA stock, a strict five for older stock.
Era, tier, and per-issuer cap computed per taxpayer, per issuer, per year before any exit modeling goes out.
risks: The leading failure mode is proof, not law: qualification is fixed at issuance but examined years later, and a missing gross-assets balance sheet from the issuance date is the most common way the exclusion dies — with no marquee taxpayer-victory case to lean on, the file is the defense.

Excluded-field characterization is contested at the margins — consulting-adjacent and professional-services-adjacent businesses need a hard, documented look at §1202(e)(3) before the exclusion is promised.
Cap multiplication through gifts draws step-transaction and donative-intent scrutiny; gifts completed while a sale process is underway are the fact pattern that fails.
Two regimes now run in parallel, and confusing a client's pre- versus post-July 5, 2025 lots misstates both the tier and the cap.
Partial tiers carry the 7% AMT preference and 28%-rate tax on the included portion — modeled benefits that ignore them are overstated, and this engine computes neither.
Significant issuer redemptions around the issuance window can disqualify the stock retroactively.
stateNotes: State conformity is the swing variable: several states — California most prominently — decline to conform to §1202 at all, so the state tax can be the entire bill; the founder's state of residence at sale matters as much as the holding period.
No PTET interaction — the exclusion applies to an individual's capital gain on stock, outside any entity-level tax election.

Missouri is fully favorable: it conforms through the federal-AGI starting point (RSMo §143.121), so excluded gain never reaches the Missouri return, and the 2025 individual capital-gains subtraction (HB 594) removes any taxable remainder for Missouri residents.
reviewChecklist: Each lot's era determined (pre- vs. post-July 5, 2025) with the matching ceiling, cap, and tier schedule.
The issuance-date proof file exists — gross-assets balance sheet, board records, QSBS representation letter — or is commissioned now, years ahead of any exit.
The per-issuer, per-taxpayer cap is computed, and the modeled eligible gain equals the post-tier excludable amount within it.
The active-business and excluded-field analysis is documented across the full holding period, including any redemption history.
Any cap-multiplication gifting is vetted with estate counsel and completed well before a sale process opens.
State exposure is priced for nonconforming states, especially for founders weighing a move before sale.

client.teaser: The right startup shares can make millions of gain free of federal tax.
client.headline: Startup stock that can be tax-free when you sell
plainEnglish: The tax law rewards early bets on small American companies. If you got shares straight from a small company — not bought from someone else — and you hold them long enough, a huge part of your profit can be free of federal tax when you sell.

For shares issued after July 2025, the break builds in stages. Hold three years and half the profit is tax-free. Four years, three quarters. Five years, all of it — up to a cap of $15 million or more per company. Older shares follow the old rule: a full five years, with a $10 million cap.

The hard part is proof and patience. The company had to qualify when you got the shares, and proving that years later is tough. We build the proof file early, track each block's dates, and time each sale to land on the best tier.
client.analogy: It works like a savings bond that matures in stages. Cash out early and you leave most of the prize behind. Wait for full maturity and the whole gain can be yours, free of federal tax.
benefits: Up to 100% of the profit on qualifying shares free of federal tax
Caps of $15 million or more per company — life-changing money, not a rounding error
Sale timing planned around the three-, four-, and five-year milestones
Advanced options can spread the cap across family members
steps: WE confirm whether each block of shares qualifies and build the proof file.
WE calendar the holding-period milestones for every block you own.
YOU hold to the plan — selling even a little early can cost most of the break.
WE model each sale date in dollars and handle the special reporting when you sell.
clientCommitments: Save every issuance document now — proof gets harder each year
Talk to us before any sale, secondary offer, or company buyback of shares

annualMaintenance: Monitor the active-business test and redemption activity with the company each year
Update the lot calendar as tier dates approach
Re-verify era, tier, and cap before any sale process opens
deliverables: QSBS qualification file — issuance balance sheet, representation letter, cap table history
Exit modeling memo pricing each sale date in dollars

suggest.reason: Original-issue C-corp stock held five years can exclude gain up to the §1202 ceiling.
